subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Quantitative and qualitative methods (surveys, interviews, observation, experiments)

questions.q: What are primary data in sociological research?
options: Data collected first-hand by the researcher for their own study
Data already collected by someone else for another purpose
Data that is only ever numerical
Data taken from newspapers and diaries
questions.explain: Primary data are gathered directly by the researcher, for example through their own questionnaires, interviews or observations.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a secondary source?
options: Official government statistics
A questionnaire the researcher designs and hands out
A structured interview the researcher conducts
Observation carried out by the researcher
questions.explain: Secondary sources are pre-existing data collected by others, such as official statistics, and are not gathered first-hand by the researcher.

questions.q: What is a key practical advantage of using secondary data?
options: It is usually cheaper and quicker because it already exists
It always gives a more valid picture than primary data
It is always more up to date than primary data
It is always collected exactly for the researcher's aims
questions.explain: Because secondary data has already been collected, using it saves the time and money involved in gathering primary data.

questions.q: What is quantitative data?
options: Data in numerical form that can be counted or measured
Data expressed in words describing feelings and meanings
Data that can only come from interviews
Data that is always unreliable
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical and can be presented in tables, charts and statistics.

questions.q: What is qualitative data?
options: Data expressed in words that describes meanings, feelings and experiences
Data that is always in the form of numbers
Data collected only from official statistics
Data that can always be turned into percentages
questions.explain: Qualitative data is descriptive, presented in words, and captures people's meanings and experiences in depth.

questions.q: A questionnaire uses only closed questions with fixed-choice answers. What type of data will this mainly produce?
options: Quantitative data
Qualitative data
Secondary data
Observational data
questions.explain: Closed, fixed-choice questions produce answers that can be counted and turned into statistics, giving quantitative data.

questions.q: What is a structured interview?
options: An interview using a set list of standardised, pre-set questions
An informal chat with no planned questions
An interview where the respondent leads the conversation
An interview carried out entirely by post
questions.explain: In a structured interview every respondent is asked the same standardised questions in the same order.

questions.q: What is a main advantage of an unstructured interview?
options: It produces rich, detailed, valid qualitative data
It is quick to carry out with very large samples
It produces data that is easy to turn into statistics
It guarantees a fully representative sample
questions.explain: The flexible, conversational style lets respondents explain their views fully, giving detailed and valid qualitative data.

questions.q: What is the main ethical problem with covert participant observation?
options: Participants have not given informed consent
It is far too expensive to carry out
It always produces only quantitative data
It can only be used with very small groups
questions.explain: Because the researcher hides their identity and purpose, participants cannot give informed consent, which is a serious ethical issue.

questions.q: Where is a laboratory experiment carried out?
options: In an artificial, controlled environment set up by the researcher
In the participants' own natural, everyday setting
Only through the post using questionnaires
Using official statistics gathered by the government
questions.explain: A laboratory experiment takes place in a controlled setting where the researcher can control variables, unlike a field experiment in a natural setting.

questions.q: A researcher wants to collect statistical data on the attitudes of several thousand people across the country quickly and cheaply. Which method is most suitable?
options: A postal or online questionnaire (survey)
In-depth unstructured interviews
Covert participant observation
A small laboratory experiment
questions.explain: Surveys using questionnaires can reach very large, geographically spread samples cheaply and produce quantitative data.

questions.q: A sociologist wants to understand in depth the feelings and experiences of a small group of young carers. Which method is most appropriate?
options: Unstructured interviews
A closed-question survey of thousands of people
A laboratory experiment
Analysis of national statistics only
questions.explain: Unstructured interviews allow detailed, in-depth exploration of meanings and experiences, giving valid qualitative data.

questions.q: What is a sampling frame?
options: A list of all the members of the population being studied
The final sample chosen for the research
The set of questions asked in a survey
The controlled setting used in an experiment
questions.explain: A sampling frame is a complete list of the research population from which a sample is drawn, such as a school register.

questions.q: In random sampling, what is true of every member of the sampling frame?
options: Each has an equal chance of being selected
Each is chosen by the researcher personally
Each must volunteer to take part
Each is picked because they are easy to reach
questions.explain: Random sampling gives every member of the sampling frame an equal chance of being chosen, reducing researcher bias.

questions.q: What is the purpose of stratified sampling?
options: To make sure key groups appear in the sample in the same proportion as in the population
To choose only people who are easiest to contact
To let each new participant name the next one
To avoid using a sampling frame at all
questions.explain: Stratified sampling divides the population into groups and samples each in proportion, improving representativeness.

questions.q: Why might a researcher use snowball sampling?
options: To reach hard-to-find groups by asking participants to suggest others
Because it always produces a fully representative sample
Because it gives everyone an equal chance of selection
Because it is the only method that produces numerical data
questions.explain: Snowball sampling is useful for hard-to-reach or hidden groups, as existing participants introduce further participants.

questions.q: A teacher puts every pupil's name into a hat and draws out 30 names for a study. Which sampling method is this?
options: Random sampling
Snowball sampling
Quota sampling
Stratified sampling
questions.explain: Drawing names blindly from a hat gives every pupil an equal chance of selection, which is random sampling.

questions.q: What does it mean if a research method is reliable?
options: If repeated, it would produce the same or very similar results
It gives a true and accurate picture of what is being studied
It uses a large and representative sample
It always uses secondary rather than primary data
questions.explain: Reliability refers to consistency: a reliable method can be repeated by others and produce the same results.

questions.q: A method is described as having high validity. What does this mean?
options: It gives a true, accurate picture of what it is meant to measure
It can easily be repeated to get the same results
It always uses a very large sample
It always produces numerical data
questions.explain: Validity means the data genuinely reflects reality and measures what the researcher intended to measure.

questions.q: A study of 20 pupils from a single school is used to make claims about all pupils in the UK. What is this sample most likely to lack?
options: Representativeness
Reliability
Numerical data
A sampling frame
questions.explain: A small sample from one school is unlikely to reflect the wider population, so generalisations from it lack representativeness.
